name: Cholecalciferol
description: Active form of Vitamin D3; fat-soluble prohormone
mechanism: Converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, then in the kidneys to the active hormone calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3). Calcitriol binds nuclear vitamin D receptors (VDR) in intestinal cells to upregulate TRPV6 calcium channels, driving active calcium absorption. VDR activation also regulates over 200 genes involved in immune modulation, cell differentiation, and bone mineralisation.

name: Ascorbic Acid
description: Bioavailable form of Vitamin C; water-soluble antioxidant
mechanism: Acts as an electron donor, regenerating oxidised antioxidants such as alpha-tocopherol and serving as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases required for collagen cross-linking. Reduces ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺) in the intestinal lumen, enhancing non-haem iron uptake. Also scavenges superoxide, hydroxyl radicals, and hypochlorous acid, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

name: Thiamine Mononitrate
description: Stable salt form of Vitamin B1
mechanism: Hydrolysed to free thiamine and phosphorylated intracellularly to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active coenzyme form. TPP is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle for ATP production. Also activates transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway, supporting nucleotide synthesis and NADPH regeneration.

name: Riboflavin
description: Active form of Vitamin B2; yellow flavin coenzyme
mechanism: Phosphorylated to flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), two redox coenzymes central to the mitochondrial electron transport chain (Complexes I and II). FAD is additionally required for glutathione reductase, maintaining the cellular antioxidant pool, and for the activation of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine → PLP) and folate into their active coenzyme forms. Without adequate riboflavin, the function of multiple other B vitamins is impaired.

name: Nicotinamide
description: Non-flush form of Vitamin B3; NAD+ precursor
mechanism: Incorporated into NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, coenzymes participating in over 400 enzymatic redox reactions including glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and beta-oxidation of fatty acids. NAD⁺ also serves as the obligate substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1–7) and PARP enzymes involved in DNA repair, chromatin remodelling, and cellular stress responses. Because it bypasses the GPR109A receptor, nicotinamide does not cause the prostaglandin-mediated flushing seen with nicotinic acid.

name: Nicotinic Acid
description: Direct NAD+ precursor; flush-inducing form of B3
mechanism: Converted to NAD⁺ via the Preiss-Handler pathway, providing the same redox coenzyme function as nicotinamide across all NAD⁺-dependent reactions. At pharmacological doses, activates the GPR109A receptor on Langerhans cells in the skin, triggering prostaglandin D2 and E2 release that causes the characteristic skin flush. Also inhibits hepatic diacylglycerol acyltransferase-2 (DGAT-2), reducing VLDL secretion and lowering plasma triglycerides.

name: Calcium D-Pantothenate
description: Salt form of Vitamin B5 used in CoA synthesis
mechanism: Converted stepwise to 4-phosphopantetheine and incorporated into coenzyme A (CoA) and acyl carrier protein (ACP). CoA is the universal thioester-forming cofactor required for fatty acid beta-oxidation, acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle, and the synthesis of steroid hormones, haem, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. ACP is indispensable for the fatty acid synthase (FAS) complex in de novo lipid synthesis.

name: Pyridoxine HCl
description: Standard supplemental form of Vitamin B6
mechanism: Phosphorylated to pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP), the active cofactor for over 100 enzyme reactions involving amino acid metabolism, including transamination (alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase) and decarboxylation. PLP is essential for the synthesis of serotonin (from tryptophan), dopamine and norepinephrine (from DOPA), GABA (from glutamate), and haem (via delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase). It also supports glycogen phosphorylase, enabling hepatic glycogen mobilisation during fasting.

name: Cyanocobalamin
description: Synthetic form of Vitamin B12; converts to active coenzyme form
mechanism: Converted in tissues to two active coenzyme forms: methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin. Methylcobalamin is the cofactor for methionine synthase, remethylating homocysteine to methionine and regenerating active tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis. Adenosylcobalamin supports methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in the catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids, and is critical for myelin sheath synthesis and maintenance.

name: D-Biotin
description: Biologically active form of Biotin; coenzyme for carboxylases
mechanism: Functions as a covalently bound prosthetic group on four human carboxylase enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase (gluconeogenesis), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (fatty acid synthesis), propionyl-CoA carboxylase (amino acid catabolism), and beta-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (leucine degradation). Each enzyme uses biotin to ferry activated CO₂ between metabolic intermediates, making it essential across energy substrate metabolism. Biotin is also involved in epigenetic regulation via biotinylation of histone lysine residues.

name: Pteroylmonoglutamic Acid
description: Synthetic folate used in supplements
mechanism: Reduced sequentially to dihydrofolate (DHF) then tetrahydrofolate (THF) by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). THF-derived one-carbon units are essential for de novo purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) biosynthesis, making folate indispensable for DNA replication in rapidly dividing cells. 5-methylTHF also donates its methyl group to cobalamin for homocysteine remethylation; deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and, in early pregnancy, neural tube defects.

name: Retinyl Palmitate
description: Preformed Vitamin A ester; fat-soluble
mechanism: Hydrolysed in the gut to retinol, taken up by enterocytes, re-esterified, and delivered to the liver via chylomicrons. Retinol is oxidised to retinoic acid, which binds nuclear RAR and RXR receptors to regulate transcription of genes governing epithelial cell differentiation, immune cell maturation (T-cell development), and reproduction. 11-cis-retinal, a separate metabolite, is the chromophore in rod cell opsin required for dim-light vision.

name: d-alpha-Tocopherol
description: Natural form of Vitamin E; most bioactive tocopherol isomer
mechanism: Preferentially incorporated into cell membrane phospholipid bilayers due to its long phytyl tail, where it intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) by donating a hydrogen atom, breaking the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation. The resulting tocopheroxyl radical is recycled back to active vitamin E by ascorbic acid and glutathione. Also modulates protein kinase C (PKC) activity and inhibits platelet aggregation via prostaglandin I2 upregulation, independently of its antioxidant role.

name: Phylloquinone
description: Vitamin K1; plant-derived blood-clotting cofactor
mechanism: Serves as the obligate cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which carboxylates specific glutamate residues on vitamin K-dependent proteins, adding calcium-binding capacity. In blood coagulation, this activates clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X and anticoagulant proteins C and S, enabling the haemostatic cascade to function at sites of vascular injury. Phylloquinone's shorter side chain gives it a short half-life and primary activity in hepatic clotting factor synthesis.

name: Menaquinone-7 (MK-7)
description: Long-chain Vitamin K2; bone and cardiovascular form
mechanism: Same gamma-glutamyl carboxylase cofactor mechanism as K1, but MK-7's seven-isoprenoid side chain confers a plasma half-life of approximately 72 hours versus 1–2 hours for K1, enabling broader tissue distribution. In bone, activates osteocalcin in osteoblasts to bind calcium within hydroxyapatite; in arterial walls, activates matrix Gla protein (MGP) to inhibit vascular calcification by sequestering calcium away from smooth muscle. These extrahepatic effects are poorly achieved by phylloquinone at dietary intakes.

name: Magnesium Oxide
description: High elemental magnesium; standard supplement form
mechanism: Dissociates in gastric acid to release Mg²⁺ ions for intestinal absorption. Magnesium is a cofactor for over 300 enzymes, most critically as part of the Mg-ATP complex required for all phosphotransferase (kinase and ATPase) reactions, including the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump that maintains membrane potential. Also regulates NMDA glutamate receptor gating as a voltage-dependent channel blocker, and opposes calcium in smooth muscle relaxation.

name: Magnesium Bisglycinate
description: Amino acid chelate; highly bioavailable and gentle
mechanism: The glycinate chelation protects Mg²⁺ from competing ions (calcium, phosphate, phytate) in the gut lumen, improving absorption via dipeptide (PepT1) and amino acid transporter pathways alongside the classic paracellular route. Exerts the same downstream cofactor functions as elemental magnesium — Mg-ATP complex formation, enzyme activation, and NMDA receptor modulation — with minimal osmotic laxative effect compared to oxide and sulfate salts. Preferred in individuals with sensitive digestion or high therapeutic magnesium requirements.

name: Magnesium Citrate
description: Organic salt; well absorbed and gentle on digestion
mechanism: Citrate increases Mg²⁺ solubility across a wide intestinal pH range, facilitating both passive paracellular and active transcellular absorption. Absorbed citrate is metabolised to bicarbonate, mildly alkalinising the urine and reducing urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation, which may lower renal stone risk as a secondary benefit. Provides the same Mg-ATP complex and enzyme cofactor functions as other magnesium salts once absorbed.

name: Ferrous Sulfate
description: Standard iron salt; high elemental iron content
mechanism: Fe²⁺ is absorbed across the duodenal brush border via the divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), enters the portal circulation bound to transferrin (as Fe³⁺), and is delivered to bone marrow erythroid precursors. Within developing red cells, iron is inserted into protoporphyrin IX by ferrochelatase to form haem, the oxygen-carrying core of haemoglobin. Iron also forms the catalytic centres of electron transport chain complexes (I, II, III) and iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, underpinning mitochondrial ATP production.

name: Ferrous Fumarate
description: Organic iron salt; better tolerated than sulfate
mechanism: Fe²⁺ is absorbed via the same DMT1 transporter pathway as ferrous sulfate and delivers identical downstream haem biosynthesis and electron transport chain functions. The fumarate anion is an endogenous TCA cycle intermediate that is rapidly metabolised once absorbed, conferring modestly better gastrointestinal tolerability than the sulfate salt without altering iron absorption efficiency. Preferred in patients who experience GI side effects from ferrous sulfate.

name: Zinc Gluconate
description: Well-absorbed organic zinc salt
mechanism: Zn²⁺ ions dissociate in gastric acid and are absorbed via ZIP4 transporters in the enterocyte apical membrane; absorption is regulated by metallothionein and ZnT1 export proteins. Zinc serves as a catalytic or structural component in over 300 enzymes (including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, SOD1, and carboxypeptidases) and as the structural core of zinc finger transcription factors controlling immune cell differentiation, gene expression, and DNA repair. Critical for thymulin synthesis and T-lymphocyte maturation.

name: Calcium Carbonate
description: High-elemental calcium; requires stomach acid to absorb
mechanism: Requires gastric acid to dissociate into Ca²⁺; absorption occurs predominantly in the duodenum via calcitriol-induced TRPV6 channels (active transcellular transport) and via passive paracellular diffusion throughout the small intestine. Absorbed Ca²⁺ is the primary second messenger for muscle contraction (troponin C binding, triggering actomyosin cross-bridge cycling), synaptic neurotransmitter vesicle fusion, and intracellular signalling cascades (calmodulin-dependent kinases). Also the principal mineral in hydroxyapatite (Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂), providing structural rigidity to bone.

name: Selenomethionine
description: Organic selenium; highest bioavailability form
mechanism: Absorbed via the same sodium-dependent neutral amino acid transporter (B⁰AT1) used for methionine, achieving superior bioavailability over inorganic selenite. Selenium is co-translationally incorporated as the 21st amino acid selenocysteine into selenoproteins encoded by the UGA codon. Key selenoproteins include glutathione peroxidases (GPx1–4), which reduce hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides; thioredoxin reductases (TrxR), which regenerate thioredoxin for ribonucleotide synthesis; and iodothyronine deiodinases (DIO1/2), which convert inactive T4 to active T3.

name: Potassium Citrate
description: Bioavailable organic potassium salt
mechanism: K⁺ is the principal intracellular cation, maintained at ~140 mM inside cells by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, establishing the resting membrane potential (~−70 mV) of excitable cells essential for neuronal firing and muscle contraction. Co-transporter systems (NKCC, KCC) use the K⁺ gradient to drive sodium and chloride movement in renal tubules, determining extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. The citrate anion is metabolised to bicarbonate, alkalinising the urine and reducing calcium oxalate and uric acid stone formation.

name: Copper Gluconate
description: Bioavailable copper salt for enzyme function
mechanism: Cu²⁺ is the catalytic centre of several cuproenzymes: cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, reducing O₂ to water); superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1, the cytosolic antioxidant enzyme); lysyl oxidase (cross-linking collagen and elastin for connective tissue tensile strength); and dopamine beta-hydroxylase (converting dopamine to norepinephrine). Ceruloplasmin, the major copper-transport plasma protein, also acts as a ferroxidase, oxidising Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ for transferrin loading, linking copper status to iron metabolism.

name: Chromium Picolinate
description: Picolinic acid chelate supporting glucose metabolism
mechanism: Picolinic acid chelation enhances intestinal Cr³⁺ absorption compared to inorganic chromium salts. Absorbed chromium is proposed to bind to a low-molecular-weight chromium-binding substance (chromodulin/LMWCr) in the cytosol of insulin-responsive cells, which then activates the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase, amplifying GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Evidence from meta-analyses (primarily in type 2 diabetes) supports modest improvements in fasting glucose; EFSA has not authorised a health claim pending further mechanistic evidence.

name: Potassium Iodide
description: Inorganic iodine salt for thyroid hormone synthesis
mechanism: Iodide is actively concentrated in thyroid follicular cells up to 20–40-fold above plasma levels via the basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS). Within the follicular lumen, thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide and catalyses its organification onto tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin, forming mono- and di-iodotyrosines that couple to yield thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors (TRα/TRβ) to regulate metabolic rate, thermogenesis, cardiac output, and development of the fetal nervous system.

name: Boron Citrate
description: Organic boron compound for bone and joint metabolism
mechanism: Boron is not yet classified as an essential nutrient with a defined biochemical mechanism, but acts as a reversible covalent inhibitor of enzymes that use NAD⁺ as a substrate, and modulates the activity of hydroxylation enzymes involved in steroid hormone metabolism. Dietary boron supplementation has been shown to increase plasma oestradiol, testosterone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 concentrations, and to reduce urinary calcium and magnesium excretion, suggesting a regulatory role in mineral and hormone homeostasis. Also proposed to modulate the NF-κB inflammatory pathway.

name: Manganese Gluconate
description: Bioavailable manganese salt for enzyme activation
mechanism: Mn²⁺ is the essential catalytic metal for manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD/SOD2), the primary mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme that dismutates superoxide anions generated by the electron transport chain. Also functions as a cofactor for arginase (converting arginine to ornithine and urea in the hepatic urea cycle), pyruvate carboxylase (gluconeogenesis initiation), and glycosyltransferases responsible for the synthesis of proteoglycans in cartilage extracellular matrix. Absorbed via DMT1 transporter pathways shared with iron.

name: Sodium Chloride
description: Primary electrolyte for fluid and nerve function
mechanism: Na⁺ is the principal extracellular cation and the primary determinant of plasma osmolality and extracellular fluid volume, regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and ADH. The electrochemical Na⁺ gradient established by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase drives secondary active co-transport of glucose (SGLT1), amino acids, and other nutrients across intestinal and renal epithelia. Rapid depolarisation of neuronal and cardiomyocyte membranes via voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (Nav) underlies the generation and propagation of action potentials.

name: Withanolides
description: Steroidal lactones; key bioactives standardised from ashwagandha root
mechanism: Withanolides are steroidal lactones structurally analogous to glucocorticoids that bind and inhibit IκB kinase (IKK), blocking NF-κB nuclear translocation and suppressing transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and stress-response genes. They also modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, reducing cortisol secretion and down-regulating heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90), which is required for glucocorticoid receptor stabilisation. GABA-mimetic activity at GABAA receptors contributes to the anxiolytic effects demonstrated in randomised controlled trials.

name: Ginkgo Flavone Glycosides
description: Antioxidant flavonoids standardised from Ginkgo biloba
mechanism: Quercetin, kaempferol, and isorhamnetin glycosides act as free-radical scavengers, donating electrons to neutralise superoxide and hydroxyl radicals, thereby reducing oxidative stress in neuronal and vascular tissue. They also inhibit platelet-activating factor (PAF) by competing at its receptor, reducing platelet aggregation and cerebrovascular inflammation. Flavonoid-mediated inhibition of phosphodiesterase (PDE) increases intracellular cAMP, promoting nitric-oxide-dependent vasodilation and improved cerebral blood flow.

name: Terpene Lactones
description: Diterpenes (ginkgolides/bilobalide) from Ginkgo biloba
mechanism: Ginkgolides A, B, and C are potent and selective antagonists of the platelet-activating factor (PAF) receptor, inhibiting PAF-induced platelet aggregation, neutrophil activation, and neuroinflammation at nanomolar concentrations. Bilobalide protects mitochondrial membrane integrity under ischaemic conditions and promotes neuronal survival by inhibiting glutamate-induced NMDA receptor excitotoxicity. Together with the flavone glycosides, the terpene lactones form the pharmacological basis of standardised Ginkgo biloba leaf extract (EGb 761).

name: Hypericin
description: Naphthodianthrone pigment from St John's Wort
mechanism: Hypericin and pseudohypericin inhibit monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) and MAO-B in vitro, reducing the degradation of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft. Hypericin also activates sigma-1 receptors, which modulate neuroplasticity and neuroprotection, and influences pineal melatonin secretion, potentially contributing to effects on sleep and mood regulation. Its photosensitising properties arise from the generation of singlet oxygen upon light exposure, which has also been investigated in photodynamic antimicrobial and antiviral contexts.

name: Hyperforin
description: Phloroglucinol compound; mood-modulating active in St John's Wort
mechanism: The primary antidepressant constituent of St John's Wort; inhibits neuronal reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, GABA, and glutamate through a mechanism distinct from conventional SSRIs. Hyperforin activates transient receptor potential canonical 6 (TRPC6) channels, causing Na⁺ influx and membrane depolarisation that reduces the driving force for monoamine transporters, increasing synaptic availability of multiple neurotransmitters simultaneously. Clinical trials and Cochrane reviews support efficacy equivalent to standard antidepressants for mild-to-moderate depression.

name: Cannabidiol (CBD)
description: Non-psychoactive cannabinoid from hemp extract
mechanism: Acts as a negative allosteric modulator of CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors, reducing their signalling without direct agonism, and thus lacking the psychoactive effects of THC. Simultaneously acts as an agonist at TRPV1 (vanilloid receptor, involved in pain and temperature), 5-HT1A serotonin receptors (anxiolytic and antiemetic effects), and GPR55 receptors. Inhibits fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), preventing the breakdown of endocannabinoid anandamide, thereby amplifying endogenous cannabinoid tone.

name: L-Theanine
description: Non-protein amino acid from green tea; promotes calm alertness
mechanism: Crosses the blood-brain barrier via the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1) and antagonises ionotropic glutamate receptors (NMDA, AMPA, and kainate), reducing excitatory neurotransmission. Simultaneously increases brain serotonin and GABA concentrations and dose-dependently promotes alpha-wave electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, which is associated with a state of alert relaxation without drowsiness. Human trials show synergistic effects with caffeine on attention and reaction time, including in studies conducted at the University of Surrey.

name: Beta-Glucans
description: Immunomodulatory polysaccharides from Lion's Mane mushroom
mechanism: (1→3),(1→4)-beta-D-glucans from Hericium erinaceus are recognised by Dectin-1 and TLR-2 pattern recognition receptors on innate immune cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils), triggering Syk-kinase-mediated signalling and innate immune activation. This leads to enhanced phagocytosis, cytokine secretion (IL-12, TNF-α), and downstream priming of adaptive T-cell responses. Some beta-glucan fractions also modulate the gut microbiome as prebiotic fibres, selectively enriching Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus.

name: Hericenones
description: Aromatic compounds from Lion's Mane fruiting body
mechanism: Hericenones C, D, E, F, G, and H are isoindolinone-type aromatic compounds found exclusively in the fruiting body of Hericium erinaceus. They cross the blood-brain barrier and stimulate the synthesis and secretion of nerve growth factor (NGF) from astrocytes and neuronal cells via an as-yet uncharacterised receptor-mediated pathway. NGF activates TrkA (tropomyosin receptor kinase A) and p75NTR receptors, promoting cholinergic neuron survival, axonal sprouting, and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.

name: Erinacines
description: Diterpenoids from Lion's Mane mycelium; stimulate nerve growth factor
mechanism: Erinacines A, B, C, and I are cyathane-type diterpenoids found exclusively in the mycelium of Hericium erinaceus. They penetrate the blood-brain barrier and potently stimulate de novo NGF synthesis in the hippocampus and cerebellum, with erinacine A acting on locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons to increase catecholamine turnover. The resulting NGF elevation activates TrkA signalling pathways supporting peripheral and central neuronal survival, differentiation, and the maintenance of cholinergic neurons relevant to memory and learning.

name: Eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA)
description: Long-chain omega-3 for inflammation and cardiovascular health
mechanism: Incorporated into membrane phospholipids where it competes with and partially replaces arachidonic acid (AA), reducing substrate availability for pro-inflammatory prostaglandin E2, thromboxane A2, and leukotriene B4 synthesis via COX and 5-LOX pathways. Simultaneously serves as a substrate for the biosynthesis of E-series resolvins and protectins, specialised pro-resolving mediators that actively terminate inflammatory responses. Also activates PPARα and PPARγ nuclear receptors, suppressing hepatic triglyceride synthesis and inflammatory gene transcription.

name: Docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA)
description: Long-chain omega-3 for brain structure and retinal health
mechanism: Concentrated in neuronal synaptic membranes and photoreceptor outer segment phospholipids, where its multiple double bonds confer exceptional membrane fluidity essential for rapid conformational changes in G-protein-coupled receptors (particularly rhodopsin in rod cells for dim-light vision). In neurons, DHA modulates BDNF expression, synaptic plasticity, and is the precursor for neuroprotectin D1, an endogenous neuroprotective lipid mediator that inhibits pro-apoptotic signalling. DHA incorporation into retinal photoreceptor membranes during fetal and infant development is critical for visual acuity.

name: Linoleic Acid
description: Essential omega-6 fatty acid
mechanism: An essential fatty acid that cannot be synthesised de novo by humans and must be obtained from the diet. Elongated and desaturated by FADS1 and FADS2 enzymes to arachidonic acid (AA), the primary precursor for series-2 prostaglandins, thromboxane A2, and leukotriene B4 — eicosanoid signalling molecules central to the inflammatory and immune response cascade. Also incorporated into ceramide and sphingomyelin in the stratum corneum, maintaining skin barrier impermeability.

name: Oleic Acid
description: Monounsaturated omega-9 fatty acid
mechanism: Incorporated into membrane phospholipids, reducing membrane rigidity when substituting saturated fatty acids and modulating the activity of membrane-bound receptors and ion channels. Activates PPARα and PPARγ nuclear receptors, promoting fatty acid oxidation in the liver and adiponectin expression in adipocytes, respectively. Reduces LDL susceptibility to oxidative modification compared with saturated fat-enriched diets, a mechanism proposed by UK studies to underlie the cardiovascular benefits associated with Mediterranean-style dietary patterns.

name: Ubiquinone
description: Oxidised form of CoQ10; fat-soluble cellular energy carrier
mechanism: Functions as the mobile lipid-soluble electron carrier shuttling electrons from NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase (Complex I) and succinate-CoQ oxidoreductase (Complex II) to ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (Complex III) within the inner mitochondrial membrane. This electron transfer drives proton pumping across the membrane, generating the electrochemical gradient that powers ATP synthase (Complex V) for oxidative phosphorylation. The ubiquinol (reduced) form also acts as a lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant, protecting mitochondrial membranes from lipid peroxidation.

name: Allicin
description: Thiosulfinate bioactive formed from alliin in garlic
mechanism: Formed enzymatically from alliin by alliinase upon crushing or cutting garlic; allicin reacts with cysteine-containing bacterial enzymes via thiol-disulfide exchange, irreversibly inactivating acetyl-CoA synthetase and other cysteine proteases, underpinning its broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis, and induces endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), increasing NO-mediated vasodilation. Allicin also inhibits platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis, reducing platelet aggregation independently of aspirin pathways.

name: Phosphatidylcholine
description: Phospholipid carrier from krill; enhances omega-3 absorption
mechanism: EPA and DHA esterified to phosphatidylcholine (PC) are absorbed via a distinct lymphatic pathway compared with triglyceride-bound omega-3s; PC-omega-3s are incorporated directly into chylomicron phospholipid fractions and appear to deliver higher bioavailability to plasma and red blood cell membranes. Phosphatidylcholine itself is the primary phospholipid of cell membranes and a major hepatic lipid export form; choline released by PC hydrolysis serves as the direct precursor for acetylcholine synthesis by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) in cholinergic neurons.

name: Trans-Resveratrol
description: Biologically active stilbene polyphenol antioxidant
mechanism: Activates SIRT1 (sirtuin-1), an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase, by acting as an allosteric activator, stimulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α deacetylation and upregulating antioxidant defences including SOD2 and catalase. Also inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes (reducing prostaglandin synthesis), suppresses NF-κB nuclear translocation, and acts as a selective oestrogen receptor beta (ERβ) agonist. Bioavailability after oral dosing is limited by rapid glucuronidation; trans-resveratrol is the biologically active isomer, as cis-resveratrol has negligible SIRT1-activating potency.

name: Betaine
description: Osmolyte from beetroot supporting methylation and circulation
mechanism: Trimethylglycine (betaine) functions as an organic osmolyte in renal tubular cells and hepatocytes, protecting against osmotic stress by accumulating intracellularly to balance extracellular hypertonicity without disrupting enzyme function. As a methyl donor, betaine transfers a methyl group to homocysteine via betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT), converting it to methionine in a folate/B12-independent pathway, thereby reducing plasma homocysteine — an established independent cardiovascular risk factor. Betaine supplementation has also been shown to increase power output in strength exercise, likely via improved intramuscular creatine synthesis.

name: Oligomeric Proanthocyanidins
description: Condensed tannins from hawthorn berry with antioxidant activity
mechanism: Oligomeric proanthocyanidins (OPCs) from Crataegus species inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), reducing angiotensin II production and thereby decreasing arteriolar vasoconstriction and vascular smooth muscle tone. They also inhibit xanthine oxidase and scavenge reactive oxygen species at the endothelium, reducing vascular oxidative stress and improving endothelial nitric oxide availability. Additionally, OPCs bind to and stabilise collagen fibres by inhibiting collagenase and elastase, protecting the structural integrity of vascular walls.

name: Vitexin-2-rhamnoside
description: Flavonoid C-glycoside standardised from hawthorn extract
mechanism: A flavone C-glycoside from Crataegus monogyna and C. laevigata that inhibits cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase (PDE3/4), increasing intracellular cAMP concentrations in cardiomyocytes. Elevated cAMP activates protein kinase A, enhancing calcium cycling and improving myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) without increasing oxygen demand proportionally. Also produces coronary arterial vasodilation via endothelium-dependent nitric oxide release, and demonstrates antioxidant activity at the myocardial endothelium.

name: Whey Protein Concentrate
description: Fast-digesting milk-derived protein fraction
mechanism: Rapidly hydrolysed by gastric and pancreatic proteases to free amino acids and di/tripeptides within 60–90 minutes, generating a fast, high peak in plasma leucine. Leucine directly activates mTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1) via the Rag GTPase–Ragulator complex on the lysosomal surface, independently of insulin, triggering phosphorylation of 4EBP1 and S6K1 to initiate ribosomal translation and net muscle protein synthesis (MPS). Whey's high leucine content (~11% of amino acids) and rapid digestion kinetics make it particularly effective for maximising post-exercise MPS.

name: Leucine
description: Branched-chain amino acid; primary trigger for muscle protein synthesis
mechanism: Directly and dose-dependently activates mTORC1 via the Rag GTPase–Ragulator complex on the lysosomal membrane, independently of growth factor signalling. mTORC1 activation phosphorylates 4E-BP1 (releasing eIF4E for cap-dependent translation initiation) and S6K1 (activating ribosomal S6 protein), collectively upregulating the rate of ribosomal mRNA translation and net muscle protein accretion. Leucine is the primary anabolic signal among the BCAAs; isoleucine and valine modulate its effect but cannot substitute for leucine in triggering mTORC1.

name: Isoleucine
description: BCAA supporting glycogen synthesis and recovery
mechanism: Promotes glucose uptake into skeletal muscle independently of insulin by stimulating GLUT1 and GLUT4 transporter translocation to the cell surface, enhancing glycogen resynthesis during post-exercise recovery. Acts synergistically with leucine in complete BCAA supplementation to amplify mTORC1-mediated muscle protein synthesis signalling and to reduce net muscle protein breakdown by suppressing the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Also catabolised directly in skeletal muscle (unlike most amino acids, which are catabolised in the liver) providing a local glucogenic and ketogenic substrate during prolonged exercise.

name: Valine
description: BCAA for muscle tissue repair and energy during exercise
mechanism: Catabolised preferentially in skeletal muscle (not the liver) by branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT) and branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) to succinyl-CoA (a TCA cycle intermediate), providing a direct anaplerotic energy substrate for working muscle during sustained aerobic exercise. Contributes to net nitrogen balance and tissue repair as part of the BCAA trio alongside leucine and isoleucine, and may reduce central fatigue during prolonged exercise by competing with tryptophan at the large neutral amino acid transporter (LAT1) for blood-brain barrier entry, limiting serotonin precursor availability.

name: Pea Protein Isolate
description: Hypoallergenic plant protein from yellow peas
mechanism: Contains all nine essential amino acids with a DIAAS (digestible indispensable amino acid score) of approximately 0.82, with methionine as the limiting amino acid. Upon digestion, releases amino acids and di/tripeptides that activate mTORC1-mediated muscle protein synthesis signalling, with leucine content (~8% of total amino acids) sufficient to trigger a near-maximal MPS response at equivalent doses to whey in resistance-trained individuals. Being hypoallergenic and free from lactose, soy isoflavones, and gluten, it is suitable for those with dairy, soy, or gluten intolerances.

name: Rice Protein Concentrate
description: Complementary plant protein from brown rice
mechanism: Brown rice protein, while lower in lysine than whey or pea protein, provides a complementary amino acid profile that meaningfully improves the overall essential amino acid score when blended with pea protein (which is lower in methionine). Digested at a moderate rate, providing a sustained amino acid availability profile. Germinated brown rice protein also contains gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) precursors that may contribute mild calming effects alongside the structural protein function.

name: Creatine Monohydrate
description: Most studied form of creatine for ATP regeneration and power output
mechanism: Taken up into skeletal and cardiac muscle via the sodium- and chloride-dependent creatine transporter (SLC6A8) and phosphorylated by creatine kinase (CK) to phosphocreatine (PCr). During maximal-intensity muscle contractions (lasting 1–10 seconds), PCr rapidly regenerates ATP from ADP, maintaining peak power output before oxidative and glycolytic pathways can fully activate. Creatine supplementation increases total intramuscular creatine and PCr stores by approximately 20%, delaying the fall in PCr-dependent power output; this is the only EFSA-authorised health claim for a sports ingredient.

name: Lysine HCl
description: Essential amino acid for protein synthesis and collagen formation
mechanism: An indispensable amino acid that is the primary limiting amino acid in most cereal-based plant proteins. Hydroxylated at specific residues by lysyl hydroxylase (a vitamin C-dependent iron enzyme) to form hydroxylysine in collagen chains; hydroxylysine residues are then oxidised by lysyl oxidase (copper-dependent) to form pyridinoline cross-links that give collagen its tensile strength. Lysine also serves as the rate-limiting precursor (with methionine) for the hepatic and renal biosynthesis of carnitine, the obligatory carrier for long-chain fatty acid entry into the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation.

name: Threonine
description: Essential amino acid for gut integrity and immune function
mechanism: An indispensable amino acid that is the most abundant amino acid in intestinal mucins, the glycoproteins secreted by goblet cells that form the protective mucus gel layer coating the gut epithelium, preventing bacterial adhesion and enterocyte damage. Threonine is also a direct precursor for glycine (via threonine aldolase) and serine, amino acids required for purine nucleotide synthesis, glutathione production, and one-carbon metabolism. Adequate threonine availability supports immunoglobulin protein structure, underpinning mucosal immune defence.

name: Hydrolyzed Collagen Peptides (Type I/III)
description: Pre-digested collagen peptides for skin and connective tissue absorption
mechanism: Small peptides generated by enzymatic hydrolysis (particularly Pro-Hyp and Gly-Pro-Hyp di- and tripeptides) resist further digestion and are absorbed intact via the intestinal oligopeptide transporter PepT1. These peptides accumulate in the dermis, cartilage, and connective tissue where they stimulate fibroblasts and chondrocytes to increase collagen and hyaluronic acid synthesis, likely via binding to the discoidin domain receptor DDR2 and stimulating TGF-β1 signalling. Clinical trials (including work published in the British Journal of Nutrition) show improvements in skin elasticity and hydration and reductions in joint pain scores.

name: L-Beta-Alanine
description: Precursor to carnosine; buffers intramuscular acid during exercise
mechanism: The rate-limiting precursor for the intramuscular synthesis of carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) by carnosine synthase in skeletal muscle, primarily in fast-twitch (type II) fibres. Carnosine functions as a physiological pH buffer (pKa ~6.83), accepting protons produced during anaerobic glycolysis to attenuate the fall in intramuscular pH during high-intensity exercise, delaying contractile failure and muscular fatigue. A systematic review and meta-analysis (Hobson et al., 2012) demonstrated significant performance improvements in exercise tasks lasting 1–4 minutes with chronic beta-alanine supplementation.

name: Lactobacillus acidophilus
description: Lactic acid bacteria for gut flora balance
mechanism: Colonises the small intestinal epithelium via adhesion to mucin and fibronectin, producing lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide that reduce luminal pH and inhibit competitive pathogenic bacteria (Clostridioides difficile, Salmonella, H. pylori). Interacts with intestinal epithelial and dendritic cells via Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), activating NF-κB-regulated cytokine responses that promote regulatory T-cell (Treg) differentiation and mucosal IgA production, reducing pro-inflammatory IL-6 and TNF-α secretion. Produces bacteriocins (acidocin, lactacin) that further limit pathogen colonisation.

name: Bifidobacterium longum
description: Beneficial bifidobacteria for gut health and immunity
mechanism: Colonises the large intestine and metabolises non-digestible oligosaccharides (inulin, FOS, GOS) via the bifid shunt pathway, producing acetic acid and lactic acid. Fermentation also yields butyrate indirectly (cross-feeding butyrogenic bacteria), which nourishes colonocytes, reinforces epithelial tight junction proteins (claudin-1, occludin, ZO-1), and signals via free fatty acid receptors FFAR2/FFAR3 on enteroendocrine cells to modulate gut-brain axis hormones (PYY, GLP-1). Reduces intestinal permeability and systemic inflammatory cytokine levels in randomised trials.

name: Inulin
description: Fructooligosaccharide prebiotic fiber from chicory root
mechanism: Resists hydrolysis by human digestive enzymes (lacks a beta-fructosidase) and reaches the colon intact, where it is selectively fermented by Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species as defined by the updated prebiotic definition (Gibson et al., 2017, Nature Reviews Gastroenterology). Fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) — primarily butyrate, propionate, and acetate — which acidify the colonic environment, inhibit pathogen growth, provide energy to colonocytes (butyrate is the preferred fuel), and signal via FFAR2 to reduce hepatic lipogenesis and improve insulin sensitivity. EFSA has authorised the health claim that chicory inulin improves bowel function by increasing stool frequency.

name: Acetic Acid
description: Active antimicrobial component of apple cider vinegar
mechanism: Dissociates to acetate and protons in the gastrointestinal lumen; in its undissociated form penetrates bacterial cell walls, acidifying the cytoplasm and disrupting energy metabolism, providing antimicrobial activity against a broad spectrum of pathogens. Absorbed acetate is converted to acetyl-CoA and metabolised via the TCA cycle; proposed mechanisms for blood glucose attenuation include delayed gastric emptying (reducing the rate of carbohydrate absorption), inhibition of salivary and pancreatic amylase activity, and AMPK activation in the liver suppressing gluconeogenesis. Evidence supports modest acute reductions in postprandial glycaemia at doses of 15–30 mL diluted vinegar.

name: L-Glutamine
description: Most abundant free amino acid; primary fuel for gut epithelial cells
mechanism: The principal nitrogen-transporting amino acid between the gut, liver, and peripheral tissues; serves as the obligate metabolic fuel for rapidly proliferating cells including enterocytes, colonocytes, and lymphocytes, which consume glutamine via glutaminolysis rather than primarily oxidising glucose. Regulates intestinal tight junction protein expression (claudin-3, occludin, and ZO-1) via EGFR and mTOR pathways, maintaining epithelial barrier integrity and reducing paracellular permeability. Also the primary precursor for glutamate and hence the tripeptide antioxidant glutathione (GSH) in both intestinal and immune cells.

name: Acemannan
description: Acetylated polysaccharide from aloe vera inner leaf gel
mechanism: A beta-(1→4)-acetylated mannan polysaccharide that resists small intestinal hydrolysis and is recognised by mannose receptors and TLR4 on macrophages and dendritic cells in the colon and lamina propria, triggering innate immune activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) that can enhance local mucosal defence. Also stimulates fibroblast proliferation and migration via upregulation of TGF-beta1 and VEGF, promoting wound healing and mucosal repair of damaged epithelium. Exhibits prebiotic-like activity by serving as a fermentable substrate for colonic microbiota.

name: Mucilage Polysaccharides
description: Hydrophilic plant gum from slippery elm inner bark
mechanism: A complex mixture of rhamnose, galactose, and glucuronic acid-containing polysaccharides that absorb large quantities of water (up to 60 times their own weight) to form a viscous, non-digestible gel upon contact with the gastrointestinal mucosa. This gel physically coats the mucosal surface, forming a protective demulcent barrier that reduces direct contact between luminal acid, pepsin, and bile with inflamed or irritated epithelial cells, providing symptomatic relief in conditions such as reflux, IBS, and intestinal inflammation. The polysaccharides also serve as a prebiotic substrate and may stimulate mucus secretion from goblet cells.

name: Orthosilicic Acid
description: Bioavailable silicon form for connective tissue and hair strength
mechanism: The monomeric, soluble form of silicon (Si(OH)₄) that is absorbed in the proximal small intestine via passive diffusion and transported in plasma at physiological concentrations of 10–30 µmol/L. Stimulates collagen type I synthesis in fibroblasts and osteoblasts via activation of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, promoting collagen cross-link formation and connective tissue tensile strength. Silicon is also incorporated into glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan matrices of cartilage and bone, and into the keratin matrix of hair cortex cells, with epidemiological associations between dietary silicon intake and bone mineral density reported in UK cohort studies.

name: Glucosamine Sulfate
description: Amino sugar for cartilage matrix synthesis and joint lubrication
mechanism: Provides the amino sugar backbone for the biosynthesis of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) — hyaluronic acid, keratan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate — which are incorporated into aggrecan and other proteoglycans of the articular cartilage extracellular matrix. Also inhibits NF-κB activation in chondrocytes, reducing transcription of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-3, MMP-13) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) that drive cartilage degradation in osteoarthritis. NICE guidance on osteoarthritis (CG177) notes that glucosamine has modest evidence for symptom relief but does not recommend it on the NHS.

name: Chondroitin Sulfate
description: Glycosaminoglycan for cartilage water retention and shock absorption
mechanism: A highly sulfated glycosaminoglycan (GAG) consisting of alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and glucuronic acid units that is covalently attached to aggrecan core protein within the cartilage extracellular matrix. The dense negative charge from sulfate groups attracts water molecules (Donnan osmotic effect), maintaining articular cartilage hydration, viscoelasticity, and compressive load-bearing capacity. Inhibits aggrecanase (ADAMTS) and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity, protecting the GAG matrix from enzymatic degradation driven by IL-1β and TNF-α in the inflammatory joint environment.

name: Curcuminoids
description: Polyphenolic pigments from turmeric rhizome; modulate inflammation pathways
mechanism: Curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, and bisdemethoxycurcumin inhibit the IκB kinase (IKK) complex, preventing NF-κB phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, thereby suppressing transcription of COX-2, iNOS, and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) across multiple cell types. Simultaneously activates the Nrf2-Keap1 antioxidant pathway, upregulating phase II detoxification enzymes (HO-1, NQO1, glutathione S-transferases) and boosting cellular antioxidant capacity. Oral bioavailability is limited by rapid glucuronidation and sulfation; co-administration with piperine (black pepper extract) inhibits glucuronidation and increases systemic curcuminoid exposure approximately 20-fold.

name: Methylsulfonylmethane
description: Bioavailable organic sulfur compound for joint and tissue support
mechanism: Provides bioavailable organic sulfur required for the post-translational synthesis of cysteine residues in cartilage and connective tissue proteins, and for glutathione biosynthesis (the primary intracellular antioxidant tripeptide). Inhibits IκB kinase and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing COX-2 expression and IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α production in synoviocytes and chondrocytes exposed to inflammatory stimuli. Also demonstrates direct free-radical scavenging activity in oxidatively stressed musculoskeletal tissue; clinical trials report reductions in joint pain and swelling with 3 g/day supplementation.

name: Harpagoside
description: Iridoid glycoside from devil's claw root with anti-inflammatory activity
mechanism: Harpagoside and its aglycone harpagogenin inhibit NF-κB nuclear translocation by stabilising IκBα, thereby blocking transcription of COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), reducing synthesis of prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and nitric oxide in inflamed tissue. Also inhibits the release of TNF-α and IL-1β from lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages via mechanisms distinct from conventional NSAIDs, without inhibiting the constitutive COX-1 isoform. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has approved a well-established use monograph for Harpagophytum procumbens in the symptomatic relief of musculoskeletal pain.

name: Anthocyanins
description: Flavonoid pigments from elderberry with antiviral and antioxidant properties
mechanism: Cyanidin-3-glucoside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside, the predominant anthocyanins in Sambucus nigra, bind directly to the haemagglutinin surface protein of influenza virions, preventing attachment to sialic acid residues on host respiratory epithelial cells and blocking cellular entry. Also stimulate production of cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8) from human monocytes, enhancing the innate immune response during early viral infection. Anthocyanins act as potent free-radical scavengers (particularly of superoxide and hydroxyl radicals), protecting respiratory epithelial cells from oxidative damage associated with respiratory infections.

name: Choline Bitartrate
description: Salt form of choline for acetylcholine synthesis and membrane support
mechanism: Choline is taken up by cholinergic neurons via the high-affinity choline transporter (CHT1) and converted to acetylcholine by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) using acetyl-CoA; acetylcholine is then stored in synaptic vesicles and released as the neurotransmitter for both peripheral (neuromuscular junction) and central cholinergic circuits (memory, attention, parasympathetic function). Also incorporated as the polar head group of phosphatidylcholine, the dominant phospholipid of all cell membranes, and serves as a methyl donor via conversion to betaine in the BHMT pathway, linking choline metabolism to one-carbon and homocysteine metabolism. EFSA has authorised health claims for choline supporting normal lipid metabolism and liver function.

name: Gamma-Linolenic Acid (GLA)
description: Omega-6 from evening primrose seed; supports hormonal and skin health
mechanism: GLA is elongated to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA) by elongase ELOVL5 in cell membranes, which serves as the direct precursor for prostaglandin E1 (PGE1). PGE1 activates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP and inhibiting platelet aggregation, reducing T-cell IL-2 production and NK cell cytotoxicity — an overall anti-inflammatory profile that competes with the pro-inflammatory AA/PGE2 pathway. DGLA incorporation into the skin phospholipid matrix also maintains the ceramide-rich lipid bilayer of the stratum corneum, reducing transepidermal water loss and supporting skin barrier integrity.

name: Diindolylmethane (DIM)
description: Condensation product of indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables
mechanism: Formed from indole-3-carbinol via acid-catalysed condensation in the stomach; DIM is absorbed and induces cytochrome P450 enzymes CYP1A1 and CYP1A2 in hepatocytes, shifting oestradiol hydroxylation from the pro-proliferative 16α-hydroxyoestrone (16α-OHE1) pathway towards the protective 2-hydroxyoestrone (2-OHE1) pathway, favourably altering the 2:16 oestrogen metabolite ratio. Also acts as a potent aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) ligand, modulating immune cell differentiation (promoting Treg over Th17 phenotypes) and inhibiting androgen receptor nuclear translocation in prostate cells.

name: Macamides
description: Fatty acid amides unique to maca root; associated with energy and mood
mechanism: Benzylamine derivatives of long-chain fatty acids unique to Lepidium meyenii; structurally analogous to endocannabinoid fatty acid amides (anandamide/AEA), they inhibit fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), the enzyme responsible for endocannabinoid degradation, thereby increasing endocannabinoid tone at CB1 and CB2 receptors. Are also proposed to modulate monoamine neurotransmitter reuptake (dopamine, norepinephrine) in the hypothalamus, potentially contributing to the pro-energetic and mood-associated effects reported in clinical trials. Direct human mechanistic studies are limited and the full receptor-level pharmacology remains under active investigation.

name: Macaenes
description: Polyunsaturated acids from maca root with adaptogenic properties
mechanism: Glucosinolate-derived polyunsaturated fatty acids (including 5-oxo C18:3 and related structures) found exclusively in maca root with proposed modulatory effects on hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis signalling. Animal studies suggest upregulation of hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, potentially contributing to increases in LH and downstream sex hormone levels; however, direct receptor-binding and enzyme-inhibition data in humans are limited. The adaptogenic profile of maca likely reflects the combined action of macaenes and macamides rather than either compound class alone.

name: Beta-Sitosterol
description: Plant sterol from saw palmetto; inhibits 5-alpha reductase
mechanism: A phytosterol that competitively inhibits both isoforms of 5-alpha reductase (SRD5A1 and SRD5A2), the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in prostate, skin, and hair follicle tissue. Reducing DHT production decreases its binding to androgen receptors in prostate stromal cells, limiting pro-proliferative signalling implicated in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Also inhibits cholesterol esterification in the prostate cell membrane, affecting receptor-lipid raft organisation. The EMA has published a well-established-use monograph for Serenoa repens extract in lower urinary tract symptoms.

name: Lauric Acid
description: Medium-chain saturated fatty acid from saw palmetto berries
mechanism: A C12 saturated fatty acid found at high concentration in the lipidosterolic extract of saw palmetto; proposed to inhibit prolactin receptor signalling in prostate epithelial cells, which otherwise upregulates 5-alpha reductase expression and activity, complementing the direct enzyme inhibition by beta-sitosterol. Also demonstrates anti-inflammatory activity by inhibiting COX-1 and COX-2 enzyme activity and modulating arachidonic acid release from prostate cell membranes. Lauric acid's medium-chain length means it is absorbed directly via the portal circulation (bypassing chylomicron formation) and rapidly metabolised as an energy substrate.

name: Protodioscin
description: Steroidal saponin from tribulus terrestris; supports luteinising hormone
mechanism: A furostanol steroidal saponin from Tribulus terrestris roots proposed to stimulate the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, increasing secretion of luteinising hormone (LH) and, secondarily, testosterone production in Leydig cells of the testes via the cAMP-PKA-StAR signalling cascade. Some evidence suggests protodioscin may also be converted peripherally to dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), a testosterone precursor. Clinical evidence for testosterone elevation in healthy eugonadal men is inconsistent and weak; EFSA has not authorised a health claim, and mechanistic human data require further robust investigation.

name: Zinc Monomethionine
description: Chelated zinc with methionine for superior absorption and retention
mechanism: Zn²⁺ chelated with L-methionine in a 1:1 complex, allowing absorption via both the zinc-specific ZIP4 transporter and the methionine-utilising neutral amino acid transporter (B⁰AT1), providing dual uptake pathways. The chelate resists forming insoluble complexes with phytate and phosphate in the gut lumen, improving net zinc bioavailability compared with inorganic zinc salts. Once absorbed, the methionine moiety serves as an essential amino acid and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) precursor for methylation reactions, providing independent nutritional value beyond the zinc delivery.

name: Magnesium Aspartate
description: Chelated magnesium with good neurological bioavailability
mechanism: Mg²⁺ chelated with aspartic acid provides absorption via both ionic Mg²⁺ transporters (TRPM6/TRPM7) and aspartate-utilising amino acid transporter pathways. Aspartate, once separated intracellularly, feeds directly into the malate-aspartate shuttle — the primary mechanism for transferring cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix — and into the urea cycle and purine synthesis, potentially synergising with magnesium's role in Mg-ATP complex formation and mitochondrial energy production. Of interest in neurological contexts as aspartate is a neurotransmitter precursor and cerebral metabolic substrate.

name: Fulvic Acid
description: Low-molecular-weight humic substance from shilajit; mineral transport aid
mechanism: A complex mixture of low-molecular-weight organic acids (molecular weight 500–2,000 Da) formed by microbial decomposition of plant organic matter in compressed Himalayan rock sediments. Contains multiple quinone/hydroquinone functional groups capable of acting as electron carriers, shuttling electrons between redox states in a manner analogous to CoQ10, potentially enhancing mitochondrial Complex I activity and cellular ATP production. Forms soluble chelate complexes with mineral cations, improving their intestinal uptake; also reported to inhibit tau protein hyperphosphorylation in neuronal cell models, relevant to neurodegenerative disease research.

name: Dibenzo-alpha-pyrones
description: Oxygenated compounds unique to authentic shilajit resin
mechanism: Dibenzo-alpha-pyrones (DBPs) and their metabolites (DBP-chromoproteins) are oxygenated heterocyclic compounds unique to authentic shilajit, first characterised by S. Ghosal. They act as electron carriers in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, recycling CoQ10 from its oxidised form (ubiquinone) back to the active reduced form (ubiquinol), thereby enhancing electron transfer efficiency at Complex I and III and increasing net ATP synthesis in skeletal muscle mitochondria. Human studies using NMR spectroscopy demonstrate increased mitochondrial ATP production and reduced post-exercise lactate accumulation with shilajit supplementation.

name: 4-Hydroxyisoleucine
description: Amino acid from fenugreek for insulin sensitisation and glucose uptake
mechanism: A non-protein amino acid found almost exclusively in fenugreek seeds that directly stimulates insulin secretion from isolated pancreatic beta cells in a glucose-dependent manner. The proposed mechanism involves closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels (K_ATP) upon entry into beta cells, causing membrane depolarisation and voltage-gated calcium channel opening — the same pathway as sulfonylurea drugs, but only activated above normal fasting glucose concentrations, reducing hypoglycaemia risk. In vivo studies in diabetic animal models show significant reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c at doses achievable from supplementation.

name: Furostanolic Saponins
description: Steroidal saponins from fenugreek supporting testosterone metabolism
mechanism: Furostanol saponins (including protodioscin, trigoneoside, and diosgenin precursors) undergo bacterial hydrolysis in the gut to yield sapogenin aglycones that are absorbed and may inhibit aromatase (CYP19A1), the enzyme converting testosterone to oestradiol, potentially shifting the androgen-oestrogen balance. Also proposed to stimulate luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion at the pituitary level, supporting Leydig cell testosterone biosynthesis. Randomised controlled trials (including Wankhede et al., 2016, J Int Soc Sports Nutr) report modest increases in free testosterone and improvements in body composition with standardised fenugreek extract.
